opus-5.5.text:
I think people often frame these as being in tension, like you either chase a high success rate on one task or you build something general that's mediocre everywhere. In my experience, it's more subtle than that, and the relationship has actually been changing as models get bigger and the data gets more diverse.

Early on, if you wanted a robot to fold laundry really well, the most effective thing was to collect a lot of very targeted demonstrations, tune the policy, and engineer the setup. You'd get great performance, but it wouldn't transfer. Move the table, change the lighting, give it a different shirt, and it falls apart. So in that regime, specialization and generalization really did feel like a trade-off.

What we've started to see with foundation-model-style approaches is that pushing hard on a few difficult tasks can actually be good for generality, if you do it the right way. Really hard, dexterous, long-horizon tasks force the model to learn things that are broadly useful: precise contact, recovering from mistakes, reasoning about deformable objects, keeping track of progress over many steps. Those capabilities aren't specific to laundry or to boxes; they show up again in many other tasks. So a hard task can be a kind of curriculum that pulls the whole model up.

The key distinction for me is whether you improve a task by changing the model and the data, or by adding task-specific hacks around it. If performance comes from hand-designed state machines, special-purpose perception, or a narrow reward that only makes sense in one setup, it usually doesn't feed back into the foundation model at all. If it comes from better data, more diverse demonstrations, better ways of incorporating corrections, or post-training methods that are generic, then the same recipe usually helps elsewhere too.

There's also a practical side. Generalization benchmarks alone can be misleading, because a model can look broadly capable but never be reliable enough for anyone to actually use. Real deployment needs high reliability on specific things. So I think of it as two loops working together: a pretrained model that's broad and has good priors, and then fine-tuning or post-training to make it really robust on tasks people care about. Ideally what you learn in the second loop, both the data and the techniques, flows back into the first, so the next base model starts from a better place.

So I wouldn't say one comes at the expense of the other. The goal is to make specialization cheap: a model general enough that getting to high performance on a new task takes a small amount of data and effort, instead of starting from scratch each time. That's really how I'd measure whether a foundation model for robotics is working.

r001.rationale: The response describes task performance and generalization as potentially reinforcing each other, but it does not liken their relationship to rising into the air by alternately stepping on one's own feet.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people often treat these as two separate goals, almost in tension with each other, and I actually see them as much more intertwined than that.

When we push hard on a specific task, say a really dexterous manipulation problem, we're forced to confront the places where the model's representations are actually weak. You discover that it doesn't really understand contact, or it's not reasoning about occlusion, or it falls apart when the lighting changes. Those failures are not task-specific problems. They are gaps in the underlying model, and the specific task is just the thing that exposed them. So in a sense, a hard, narrow task is one of the best diagnostic tools we have for generalization.

The trap is in how you fix those failures. If you fix them by collecting ten thousand more demonstrations of exactly that task, in exactly that lab, you'll get a beautiful success rate on the benchmark and you'll have learned almost nothing transferable. The model just memorizes a corridor through the problem. But if you fix them by improving the data diversity, the architecture, the way the model grounds language in action, then the gain on that task comes with gains everywhere else. So I always ask the team: when this number goes up, do we know why? If we can't explain the improvement in terms of something general the model learned, I'm skeptical that it will hold up outside the lab.

The other direction matters too. A model that generalizes broadly but can't do anything reliably is also not very useful. Real deployments need the long tail of reliability on a few things that matter, and that last stretch of robustness is often where the real learning happens. So I'd say the healthy loop is: push on specific tasks to find out what's broken, fix it in a way that's general, then verify the fix by checking whether tasks you never trained on got better. If they didn't, you probably just overfit, and you should be honest with yourself about that.

r001.rationale: The response describes task performance and generalization as intertwined and presents a diagnostic improvement loop, but it does not liken their relationship to rising into the air by alternately stepping on one's own feet.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re related, but they’re not the same thing. You can improve performance on a particular robotics task by specializing very heavily—collecting more data in the same environment, tuning for that setup—and that doesn’t necessarily make the model more capable in a new environment.

The question is what the model has to learn to get better. If success requires handling different objects, different layouts, and different ways of accomplishing a goal, then improving task performance can help build capabilities that transfer. But if there’s a shortcut specific to the setup, the model may learn that instead.

So I would measure both: how well does it perform the tasks it was trained on, and how well does it handle changes or tasks it hasn’t seen? And for robotics, I’d also ask how much additional data it needs to adapt. A foundation model might not solve every new task immediately, but if it can learn one with very little experience, that’s a meaningful form of generalization.

Specific tasks give us concrete feedback. The challenge is making sure progress on those tasks reflects something reusable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the relationship between task performance and generalization, but it does not liken that relationship to trying to rise into the air by alternately stepping on one's own feet.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re related, but improving one doesn’t automatically improve the other. You can get very good at a particular robotics task by collecting a lot of data in one setup and optimizing for that setup. But the model might be learning shortcuts that don’t transfer when you change the objects, the lighting, or the robot itself.

The question is: what did the model have to learn to get better? If it learned something reusable about geometry, contact, or how actions change the world, then better task performance can contribute to generalization. If it memorized a particular trajectory, probably much less so.

So I’d use specific tasks as a training signal, but evaluate generalization separately. Can the robot perform the same skill with unfamiliar objects? Can it combine skills in a new way? Can it adapt to an environment it hasn’t seen? We want task performance to improve because the model has developed more general capabilities, and those held-out tests help us distinguish that from simply getting better at the training setup.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task performance and generalization, but does not compare their relationship to trying to rise into the air by alternately stepping on one’s own feet.
